edition.deck: The day’s major developments, from Spain’s deadly rail crash and the UK Budget to fresh Danish reporting.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and fresh reporting. The Spanish crash and Israel’s election remain unresolved; the UK Budget is covered as one story across its measures and economic outlook.

content.headline: At least 68 dead after two high-speed trains collide in Spain
content.shortHeadline: Spain train crash kills at least 68
content.standfirst: The collision south of Madrid derailed carriages and injured dozens. The transport minister says a signalling failure and an erroneous decision to restart a train preceded the crash; investigators have yet to establish the full cause.

image.caption: Rescue workers at the site of the train crash in Toledo province.

sources.originalTitle: What we know as over 60 feared dead after two-high speed trains collide in Spain
Spain train crash: at least 64 dead after collision in Toledo province
Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network

segments.body: At least 68 people have died after two trains collided in central Spain, according to the regional government. The trains, carrying 544 passengers, were travelling from Madrid towards Andalusia. Officials say 58 people were taken to hospital, 15 in a very serious condition; the death toll could rise.

segments.title: Questions about the railway
segments.body: Transport minister Óscar Puente said a computer communications failure had triggered a red signal and stopped rail traffic. He said a control centre then wrongly authorised the Renfe train to continue, without speed restrictions, towards a stationary Iryo train. The investigation is expected to establish how the collision happened.

The crash is Spain’s second deadly collision involving Renfe and Iryo trains this year. The January disaster killed 46 people and prompted debate about maintenance and safety on the Madrid-to-Andalusia line. Rail unions had raised safety concerns before Wednesday’s crash, but its cause is not yet confirmed.

content.headline: Israel’s election leaves both main blocs short of a majority
content.shortHeadline: Israel faces coalition deadlock after election
content.standfirst: With most votes counted, neither Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc nor Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition appears able to reach the 61 seats needed to govern. Arab parties’ gains could prove pivotal, but coalition talks may be difficult.

image.caption: Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot are both short of a projected parliamentary majority.

sources.originalTitle: Coalition talks loom in Israel as Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs set to fall short of majority
How could Israel break election deadlock? Here are four scenarios
Rise of Palestinian parties in Knesset will redraw Israel’s political landscape

segments.body: With about 86% of votes counted, both the governing bloc led by Benjamin Netanyahu and the opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot appeared short of the 61 seats needed for a majority in Israel’s 120-seat Knesset. Votes from soldiers and other absentee ballots were still to be counted.

segments.title: Arab parties hold a key choice
segments.body: Arab Israeli parties were projected to win 16 to 19 seats, a strong result that could give the opposition a route to power. But Eisenkot and other opposition leaders have resisted relying on their support. The Joint List says it cannot be ignored; forming a coalition would require negotiations and compromise.

perspectives.body: The Guardian’s analysis says Ra’am may be the easier partner for Eisenkot’s bloc, while negotiations with the larger Joint List could prove harder. A minority government is another possibility, but could be fragile.

segments.body: If neither bloc can assemble a majority, Israel could face another election, as it did repeatedly between 2019 and 2022. Netanyahu would remain prime minister in a caretaker role during any political impasse. The final seat distribution and the outcome of coalition talks are not yet known.

content.headline: Ebola outbreak exceeds 10,000 cases as Africa CDC urges wider preparedness
content.shortHeadline: Ebola outbreak exceeds 10,000 cases
content.standfirst: The Africa CDC says the outbreak has spread across three African regions and warns that countries beyond the continent should strengthen preparedness. The virus has no approved treatment, and response efforts face funding and security problems.

image.caption: A map at Nigeria’s disease-control centre shows countries affected by Ebola outbreaks.

sources.originalTitle: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official

segments.body: The current Ebola outbreak has reached 10,091 reported cases, including 4,887 deaths in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, according to figures cited by the Africa CDC. Cases have also been reported in Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria. France has reported a case in a person returning from DR Congo.

segments.title: Preparedness and treatment
segments.body: Africa CDC director general Jean Kaseya called the outbreak’s geographic spread unprecedented and urged governments to strengthen preparedness and treatment capacity. The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, which has no approved treatment; vaccine trials are under way, with results expected in three to six months.

The response has been hindered by shortages of protective equipment, unpaid health workers, conflict and mistrust in affected areas. Kaseya says more than $2bn of pledged funding remains outstanding and is urging cross-border cooperation, including screening and testing at points of entry and exit.

content.headline: Flávio Bolsonaro reaches the US after Brazil orders him to surrender passport
content.shortHeadline: Flávio Bolsonaro reaches the US after leaving Brazil
content.standfirst: The defeated presidential candidate arrived in Miami with his family after travelling through Argentina and Ecuador. He missed a court-ordered deadline to surrender his passport amid a money-laundering investigation; he has not been charged in that case.

image.caption: Flávio Bolsonaro arrives at Opa-locka Executive Airport near Miami.

sources.originalTitle: Flávio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after Brazil election loss
Efter valgnederlag: Bolsonaro lander i USA

segments.body: Flávio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil’s presidential election to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, arrived in Miami with his wife and daughters after travelling from Brazil through Argentina and Ecuador. He left the airport under police escort and did not speak to reporters.

segments.title: Investigation and unanswered questions
segments.body: Brazil’s Supreme Court had been asked to order Bolsonaro’s passport retained amid an investigation into alleged money laundering. He missed a deadline to hand it over. He denies wrongdoing and has not been charged in that investigation. It remains unclear how he travelled to the border or where he was during a gap of more than 24 hours.

content.headline: Serbian police kill attacker outside Israeli embassy in Belgrade
content.shortHeadline: Attacker killed outside Israeli embassy in Belgrade
content.standfirst: Serbia’s interior minister says a young man with knives attacked a police officer outside the embassy, leaving the officer with a minor wound. Authorities have raised the national terrorism threat level as they investigate.

image.caption: Police officers stand outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade.

source.credit: Andrej ISAKOVIC / AFP via Getty Images

sources.originalTitle: Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says

segments.body: Serbian police shot dead a young man outside Israel’s embassy in Belgrade after he attacked a police officer with two knives, Interior Minister Ivica Dačić said. The officer suffered a minor wound to the face and did not need hospital treatment. No embassy staff were injured.

Dačić said the suspect was a Serbian minor who had been monitored by security services and was known as a supporter of Islamic State. The minister raised Serbia’s terrorism threat level to red alert, the highest level. The suspect’s identity and the circumstances of the attack remain under investigation.

content.headline: Dolores Huerta, US civil rights and farm workers’ rights leader, dies at 96
content.shortHeadline: Civil rights leader Dolores Huerta dies at 96
content.standfirst: Huerta co-founded the United Farm Workers Union with César Chávez and continued campaigning on immigration and voting. Earlier this year, she said Chávez had sexually abused her, allegations that emerged in a wider investigation.

sources.originalTitle: US civil rights leader Dolores Huerta dies aged 96

segments.body: Dolores Huerta, a prominent US civil rights leader, has died aged 96, her family announced. She campaigned alongside César Chávez for farm workers’ rights in the 1960s and 1970s, and co-founded the United Farm Workers Union with him.

Huerta continued activism on immigration and voting through her foundation. Earlier this year, she said Chávez had manipulated and pressured her into sex and had forced her on another occasion in the 1960s. The allegations followed a New York Times investigation; Chávez’s family said it was devastated by the reports and praised the women who came forward.

content.headline: Trump’s voter fraud claims meet evidence of rare cases ahead of US midterms
content.shortHeadline: Evidence contradicts Trump’s claims of widespread voter fraud
content.standfirst: Donald Trump has called voter fraud rampant and offered a reward for reports leading to convictions. Studies and conviction records cited by BBC Verify suggest postal-ballot fraud and non-citizen voting are rare.

sources.originalTitle: Trump says US voter fraud is 'rampant' - evidence suggests it is extremely rare

segments.body: Ahead of the 3 November midterm elections, Donald Trump has repeated claims of widespread fraud in postal voting and non-citizen voting, and offered $1m for reports that lead to convictions. Evidence examined by BBC Verify suggests both kinds of fraud are uncommon.

segments.title: What the records show
segments.body: A Brookings Institution study found an average of about four cases of postal-vote fraud for every 10 million postal ballots across four elections. The Heritage Foundation database recorded 325 convictions for fraudulent use of postal ballots over 20 years. Reuters found 73 convictions for non-citizen voting in federal courts over three decades.

Debate also continues over tighter voter-identification rules. Critics say requirements could exclude eligible voters who lack the required documents; an expert at the conservative Cato Institute told the BBC that research has not found much evidence either of fraud or of voter suppression from existing ID laws. Rules and safeguards vary between states.

content.headline: Russia faces mounting battlefield, recruitment and economic pressures
content.shortHeadline: Russia faces mounting pressures as war continues
content.standfirst: An analysis of reporting and research cited by the i Paper describes limited Russian territorial gains, heavy losses and damage to oil infrastructure. The Kremlin’s war spending is also putting pressure on households and businesses.

image.caption: Vladimir Putin faces mounting pressures as Russia continues its war in Ukraine.

sources.originalTitle: The four snowballing crises Putin refuses to acknowledge

segments.body: The Institute for the Study of War says Russian claims of major territorial gains this year exceed its assessment of the advance. The thinktank says Ukraine has regained ground in some areas. The analysis also cites Ukrainian casualty estimates of about 40,000 Russian casualties a month, which it says broadly match some Western and independent assessments.

segments.title: Pressure on people and infrastructure
segments.body: The i Paper reports that Ukrainian drone strikes have damaged Russian oil refineries, while fuel shortages and queues have affected the public. It also describes recruitment pressures and a shift towards a war economy, with higher defence spending, inflation and taxes. These pressures have not led the Kremlin to signal that it will scale back the war.

content.headline: Budget offers £100 energy payments as watchdog warns of weaker growth
content.shortHeadline: Budget brings £100 energy payments and a bleak outlook
content.standfirst: John Healey announced one-off payments for 20 million households and other measures to ease bills. The Office for Budget Responsibility cut its growth forecast for next year and warned that inflation and household pressures will remain high.

image.caption: John Healey announces his first Budget in the House of Commons.

sources.originalTitle: Budget 2026: John Healey offers £100 payments to households to help navigate ‘global economic storms’
Budget 2026: key points at a glance
How much £100 energy payment for council tax bands A-D will help vs rising bills
‘A pretty grim picture’: outlook for UK living standards slashed despite Healey’s budget
‘Grim’ squeeze on living standards as inflation surges and growth stalls in forecast
Landlords face 4% tax rise on rental income from 2027

segments.body: The chancellor said households in council tax bands A to D would receive a £100 energy payment, with equivalent funding for Scotland and Wales. He also extended the electricity-bill VAT cut to July 2027 and said gas standing charges would be abolished from 2027. The measures are intended to offer temporary help with rising energy costs.

segments.title: A strained economic outlook
segments.body: The Office for Budget Responsibility cut its forecast for UK growth next year to 1%, from 1.5% in its previous forecast, and warned inflation would be higher. It said real disposable income per person would fall slightly in the near term before recovering modestly; its forecast leaves the government with less room against its fiscal rules.

segments.title: How the package is funded
segments.body: Healey said higher bank taxes would help fund the energy support. He also announced higher tax rates on property and savings income. The OBR warned that the property tax changes risk pushing rents up over time as some landlords leave the market and rental supply tightens; the size of any effect remains uncertain.

content.headline: Tommy Robinson convicted of harassing two Daily Mail journalists
content.shortHeadline: Tommy Robinson found guilty of harassing journalists
content.standfirst: A jury found Stephen Yaxley-Lennon guilty of harassment causing fear of violence after a campaign against two reporters. He is due to be sentenced in December and could face a custodial term.

image.caption: Tommy Robinson leaves Southwark Crown Court after his conviction.

sources.originalTitle: Tommy Robinson faces up to 10 years in jail after being found guilty of harassing journalists
Tommy Robinson guilty of harassing Mail journalists

segments.body: Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, was found guilty of two counts of harassment causing fear of violence against Daily Mail journalists Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. The case followed posts and messages after the newspaper reported that Robinson was in Cyprus during the 2024 England riots.

segments.title: Threats and sentencing
segments.body: The trial heard that Robinson hired private investigators to find the journalists’ addresses, shared images of a reporter’s family and told Young, “I’m coming to get you”. The journalists and their families feared for their safety. Robinson said he wanted to put pressure on the newspaper and denied intending to cause fear. He is due back in court on 16 December for sentencing.

content.headline: Russell Brand denies rape and assault allegations as he gives evidence
content.shortHeadline: Russell Brand denies charges in trial evidence
content.standfirst: Brand told Southwark Crown Court that consent was “non-negotiable” as he answered questions about allegations by six women. He denies three rape charges, three sexual assault charges and attempted indecent assault.

image.caption: Russell Brand leaves Southwark Crown Court after giving evidence.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand tells trial he had sex obsession but that consent is ‘non-negotiable’
Russell Brand tells court allegations made friends and colleagues turn against him

segments.body: Russell Brand gave evidence at Southwark Crown Court, denying charges of rape, sexual assault and attempted indecent assault. Six women have accused him of offences between 1999 and 2009. Brand told the court consent was “non-negotiable” and rejected the allegations against him.

segments.title: Questions over his account
segments.body: Under cross-examination, Brand acknowledged being “obsessed” with sex when younger but denied setting himself a goal to sleep with 5,000 women. Prosecutors challenged his memory of past encounters and suggested it had changed after he saw evidence; Brand denied that. The trial is ongoing and no verdict has been reached.

content.headline: Newham shows how UK homelessness extends far beyond rough sleeping
content.shortHeadline: Newham’s homelessness crisis extends beyond the streets
content.standfirst: In Newham, about 30 people are regularly seen sleeping rough, while 8,250 people are registered as homeless. The borough illustrates how high rents and a shortage of social housing leave many families in temporary accommodation.

image.caption: Kat Klimova outside the council home she shares with her sister in Newham.

sources.originalTitle: Inside the homeless capital of the UK, where 1 in 18 have no housing

segments.body: Newham in east London has the highest homelessness rate in England, according to Shelter, with one in 18 residents affected. While about 30 people are regularly sleeping rough, 8,250 people are registered as homeless, many living in hostels or bed and breakfasts while waiting for permanent homes.

segments.title: Housing shortages behind the figures
segments.body: Shelter says soaring rents and a shortage of social-rent homes leave families stuck in temporary accommodation or on waiting lists. Crisis data cited in the report found only 0.4% of private rental properties listed in Newham over the previous year were affordable to someone receiving the local housing allowance.

The government has promised £432m to tackle rough sleeping and says people sleeping on the streets should be offered help by the end of the year. Local housing representatives say extra funding is welcome but will not, by itself, resolve the shortage of affordable homes or the barriers some people face in accessing support.

content.headline: Minister backs national ban on fast-growing chickens after welfare footage
content.shortHeadline: Denmark considers ban on fast-growing chickens
content.standfirst: TV 2 footage from a poultry farm showed birds with severe mobility problems and a lighting regime experts say broke the rules. The minister wants to work towards a ban, but says legal and economic questions must be examined first.

sources.originalTitle: Skjult kamera afslører dansk kyllingeproducent i at bryde loven
Minister vil forbyde turbokyllinger i Danmark

segments.body: Hidden-camera footage from a North Jutland poultry farm showed fast-growing Ross 308 chickens with serious problems standing and walking. Experts quoted by TV 2 said some birds should have been put down. The broadcaster also reported that the flock received only three hours of darkness a day, against a six-hour minimum.

segments.title: A proposed national ban
segments.body: The farm’s owner said in a written response that conditions had not been acceptable and that he had corrected the lighting programme and other procedures. Nature and animal-welfare minister Christian Rabjerg Madsen says he wants to work towards a national ban on fast-growing chickens, but first needs to examine the legal and economic effects. Several parties support a ban.

Experts link the birds’ rapid growth to leg and other health problems. The poultry industry’s representative said the footage was disturbing but maintained that welfare is generally good across Danish production; he said he could not judge whether this farm’s case was isolated. TV 2 reports that five poultry producers have been reported to police this year.

content.headline: Cyberattacks hit Danish universities as experts warn of valuable data
content.shortHeadline: Danish universities targeted in cyberattacks
content.standfirst: Recent attacks affected systems at the University of Copenhagen and the Technical University of Denmark; Aarhus University stopped another before passwords were accessed. The incidents have not been shown to be connected.

sources.originalTitle: Cyberangreb rammer universiteter på stribe: 'De er attraktive for mange aktører'

segments.body: The University of Copenhagen said hackers accessed information relating to about 525,000 people. An attack on the Technical University of Denmark may have affected up to 200,000 current and former users. Aarhus University detected and stopped an attack before passwords for about 1,700 users were accessed.

segments.title: Why universities are targeted
segments.body: Aarhus University cybersecurity professor Jens Myrup Pedersen says universities hold personal and research data that may interest criminals, foreign states or activists. He says older systems can be difficult to secure and recommends updating them, investing in cybersecurity and making security part of routine decisions about IT and access.

content.headline: Scammers use Danish death notices to target bereaved relatives
content.shortHeadline: Scammers target relatives through death notices
content.standfirst: Criminals posing as public authorities call relatives of the deceased and ask for card details or MitID verification. Police say they have received at least 50 reports or inquiries, with more cases likely unreported.

image.caption: Online death notices are being used to identify and target bereaved relatives.

sources.originalTitle: Svindlere finder ofre i dødsannoncer: – Dybt usmageligt

segments.body: Danish police say scammers are using death notices to identify bereaved relatives. Callers impersonate Udbetaling Danmark and claim the deceased left unpaid pension or other money that can be released if relatives provide card details and verify themselves with MitID.

segments.title: How to respond
segments.body: Police say at least 50 people have contacted them about the scam, while others may not have reported it. The authority says it will not call to ask for card details or MitID codes. Consumer advice cited by TV 2 urges people to read MitID prompts carefully and contact their bank or the authorities if they suspect fraud.

content.headline: Residents in Mørke still told to boil water as contamination source remains unf‌
content.shortHeadline: Mørke residents told to keep boiling tap water
content.standfirst: A contamination warning remains in force for about 1,000 people in the East Jutland town, with no source yet identified. The local waterworks says tests found no excess bacterial count in water leaving its plant.

sources.originalTitle: Brugs sælger 20 gange mere vand end normalt

segments.body: Residents in Mørke have been told to boil tap water before using it after an elevated bacterial count was found. The warning has been in place for a week, and the waterworks says it could take about another week to resolve the problem. Around 1,000 people are affected.

segments.title: Source still unknown
segments.body: The waterworks says its tests found no bacterial count above the limit in water leaving the plant, and that contamination appears somewhere between the plant and consumers. The source has not been located, so officials cannot yet say when residents will be able to drink the water without boiling it.

content.headline: Danish thinktanks say nature protection could bring economic benefits
content.shortHeadline: Thinktanks weigh costs and benefits of protecting nature
content.standfirst: A new analysis estimates that protecting and restoring nature could produce climate and environmental benefits as well as costs. Its authors caution that tourism and other benefits are uncertain and cannot simply be combined into one total.

image.caption: The Shipsters Rev stone reef near Gl. Ålbo attracts visitors.

sources.originalTitle: Ny analyse sætter kroner på mere beskyttet natur

segments.body: A report by the thinktanks Hav and Concito argues that nature protection should not be treated only as a cost. It examines potential benefits including reduced greenhouse-gas and nitrogen emissions, cleaner drinking water, less air pollution, tourism and recreational value.

segments.title: Large estimates, with caveats
segments.body: Using earlier estimates, the report puts the funding needed to protect and restore biodiversity on land and at sea at at least 207 billion kroner through 2050. It estimates avoided climate and environmental costs from land protection at 3.7 billion kroner a year in 2030 and 11 billion in 2050. These are calculations, not a single combined measure of economic gain.

The authors say estimates for tourism and recreational value are less certain, and the report does not put a national monetary value on the benefits of protecting the sea. The methods differ, so the figures cannot simply be added together. The analysis is framed against the government’s goals for protected land and sea.

content.headline: Danish data-centre industry urges new projects despite local protests
content.shortHeadline: Data-centre industry presses ahead amid local opposition
content.standfirst: Industry representatives say rising demand for computing power makes more data centres necessary, while acknowledging neighbours’ concerns about electricity use, noise and environmental impact. Several Danish projects have been paused or shelved.

image.caption: Local residents put up protest signs against a proposed data centre near Tinghøj.

sources.originalTitle: Mens protesterne vokser, vil branchen bygge flere datacentre: 'Vi har ikke noget valg'

segments.body: Local opposition has led councils in Denmark to pause or drop a growing number of data-centre projects. The industry’s director, Henrik Hansen, says more centres are still needed as demand for server capacity rises, but says development should be controlled and involve local communities.

segments.title: Power, impact and local trust
segments.body: A representative of Dansk Industri says businesses and public services depend on digital systems, and argues that expanding capacity in Denmark would limit reliance on other countries. He also says residents are entitled to clarity about electricity use, noise and environmental effects. The government is working on a data-centre strategy.

content.headline: Nordic leaders divided over calls with Putin and how Europe should speak to him
content.shortHeadline: Nordic leaders split over direct talks with Putin
content.standfirst: Finland’s president and Norway’s prime minister say they spoke with Vladimir Putin about the war and diplomacy. Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen criticises the calls as uncoordinated, while Ukraine’s president has thanked the Nordic leaders for their efforts.

image.caption: Mette Frederiksen criticises the uncoordinated calls with Vladimir Putin.

sources.originalTitle: Mens USA og Ukraine arbejder for fred, slår den europæiske alliance sprækker
Norsk redaktør: Derfor bad jeg Mette Frederiksen holde kæft

segments.body: Norway’s Jonas Gahr Støre and Finland’s Alexander Stubb said they spoke by phone with Vladimir Putin about Russia’s war against Ukraine and diplomatic efforts. Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen criticised the initiative as uncoordinated and said European countries should stay united. Volodymyr Zelenskyy thanked the Nordic leaders for their work.

segments.title: A dispute over Europe’s role
segments.body: Aftenposten political editor Kjetil B. Alstadheim argues that Europe should have direct contact with Putin because the war is taking place on European territory and the US currently leads much of the contact. Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson, like Frederiksen, has warned that uncoordinated talks risk weakening a common European position.

perspectives.body: Alstadheim says the call was not simply a break with Ukraine’s position: Zelenskyy had been in contact with Stubb and Støre beforehand and later thanked them. He argues that Europe should be more directly involved in discussions about a war on its continent.

content.headline: Peven Everett is ready for his long-awaited moment
content.shortHeadline: Peven Everett is ready for his moment
content.standfirst: After treatment for stage-four lung cancer, the Chicago musician is returning to the stage and becoming the subject of a new documentary. His story reaches far beyond the house classic “Gabriel”.

image.caption: Peven Everett, the Chicago house and soul musician.

sources.originalTitle: ‘I knead the audience, like a baker!’ House music legend Peven Everett on life after cancer and vanquishing the ‘Disco Sucks’ movement

segments.body: Peven Everett’s “Gabriel”, co-created with producer Roy Davis Jr, became a UK club classic in the mid-1990s. But the Chicago musician’s catalogue runs to more than 500 tracks across house, soul, hip-hop and other styles, and his improvised performances resist a fixed set list. Damon Albarn calls Everett’s voice “once-in-a-generation”; Gilles Peterson compares him to Prince.

segments.title: A career on his own terms
segments.body: Everett says his career was gathering pace when he was diagnosed with stage-four lung cancer two years ago. He has completed treatment, and Denholm Hewlett’s documentary follows his life from child trumpet prodigy to self-releasing musician. Everett says he is glad to retain control of his catalogue and still enjoy making music; Hewlett thinks he is “just getting started”.

content.headline: The Nerves’ forgotten story, and a bid to bring their songs into view
content.shortHeadline: The Nerves’ songs may finally get a wider hearing
content.standfirst: The band behind Blondie’s “Hanging on the Telephone” never found the success their songs seemed to promise. A new anthology, pursued by guitarist Jack Lee’s daughter, could bring their work back into circulation.

image.caption: The Nerves’ Peter Case, Jack Lee and Paul Collins in 1975.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We did everything wrong!’ The tragedy of the hit-free band behind Blondie’s Hanging on the Telephone

segments.body: The Nerves wrote the song Blondie later made famous as “Hanging on the Telephone”, but the trio’s own career remained largely below the radar. Paul Collins, Peter Case and Jack Lee rehearsed relentlessly, pressed their own EP and toured with bands including Devo and the Ramones before splitting in 1978.

segments.title: A legacy still being assembled
segments.body: Lee’s daughter, Cynthia Cook, says her father asked her to pursue his dream of releasing an anthology on Jack White’s Third Man Records. She has found cassettes spanning several decades and estimates there is about three albums’ worth of releasable material, including recordings rescued from fans and a tape discovered in a closet. Case reflects that the band got some things wrong and others right, and that the music remains.

content.headline: Thea Gilmore turns anonymous confessions into songs—with care
content.shortHeadline: Thea Gilmore makes songs from strangers’ stories
content.standfirst: For The Echo Line, the British singer-songwriter invites anonymous messages and builds songs from the stories people share. She says the project has changed how she thinks about songwriting—and carries a responsibility to honour other people’s pain.

image.caption: Thea Gilmore, whose project The Echo Line turns anonymous messages into songs.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s not my pain. There’s a responsibility in that’: Thea Gilmore on writing songs from anonymous confessional voicemails

segments.body: After releasing 22 albums, Thea Gilmore wanted a break from writing about herself. Through The Echo Line, people can send anonymous voicemails or written messages about anything from grief and family estrangement to joy. Gilmore listens to each one, then writes a song inspired by one or more contributions; the project has received thousands of messages.

segments.title: Listening as part of the work
segments.body: Gilmore says anonymity is essential to making the project a safe place to speak. Her songs draw on stories she is trusted with, including a piece shaped by messages from a blood-bike worker, an NHS nurse and a mother whose daughter was born prematurely. “It’s not my pain,” she says, describing the weight of trying to do other people’s lives justice.

content.headline: Brian Jones’s letter recruiting Charlie Watts is going to auction
content.shortHeadline: Brian Jones’s letter to Charlie Watts goes to auction
content.standfirst: A 1962 letter from Brian Jones asks the future Rolling Stones drummer to leave Blues Incorporated for his fledgling band. Preserved by Watts’s family for more than six decades, it will be shown publicly before a December sale.

image.caption: Brian Jones, Charlie Watts, Keith Richards, Mick Jagger and Bill Wyman.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Dear Charlie’: letter revealing move to snare future Rolling Stones drummer up for auction

segments.body: In the letter, Brian Jones asks Charlie Watts to join his band, which had not yet been named the Rolling Stones. Jones says they are looking for a good drummer and boasts that the group is already “far better” than Alexis Korner’s Blues Incorporated. In a postscript, he calls their current drummer “atrocious”.

segments.title: A glimpse of the early lineup
segments.body: Watts was still working in advertising when Jones wrote to him at his childhood home in Wembley. He joined the Stones seven months later, in January 1963. The letter, which Sotheby’s says came directly from Watts’s sister, will be on public view in New York from 2 to 8 December; online bidding runs until the Rock & Pop sale on 15 December.

content.headline: Amy Winehouse’s Back to Black gets a revealing anniversary reissue
content.shortHeadline: Back to Black’s anniversary set adds a few new clues
content.standfirst: A 20th-anniversary edition gathers demos, B-sides and a concert recording around Winehouse’s landmark breakup album. The review finds intriguing glimpses of its making, while noting that the new material is limited.

sources.originalTitle: Back to Black (20th Anniversary Edition)

segments.body: The new edition of Back to Black includes previously unheard versions of songs such as “Me & Mr Jones” and “Tears Dry on Their Own”, tracing the album’s shift toward the retro-soul sound that Mark Ronson and Winehouse developed. Demos and B-sides also show the singer’s versatility, while the familiar album remains the centrepiece.

segments.title: What an archive can—and cannot—restore
segments.body: The review hears the album as intensely personal, with the relationship behind it shaping much of the songwriting. The anniversary package also includes a 2007 Amsterdam concert and previously available recordings, but only five unheard tracks. The review notes that material for a planned follow-up was destroyed, a reminder that no reissue can fill the absence of new work.

content.headline: Mackeeper’s Believe You Me turns early-2000s pop into clever indie mischief
content.shortHeadline: Mackeeper make a mischievous case for pop
content.standfirst: On their debut album, the New York duo combine rap-rock bravado, indie-pop hooks and deliberately cheeky performance. The review finds that their knowing jokes about pop never stop the songs from working.

sources.originalTitle: Believe You Me

segments.body: Brothers Miles Cohen and Nick Harwood make songs that borrow from the early 2000s—guitar-led rap, arena-rock swagger and glossy pop—without treating those references as mere nostalgia. The review singles out “Men in Black” and “Vision” for the way their tightly arranged hooks balance the duo’s mischievous, self-aware persona.

Mackeeper are unusually open about wanting their songs to be popular, and the album keeps pointing out how pop hooks work even as it invites listeners to enjoy them. The review’s verdict is that the wink does not cancel the pleasure: the duo reveal the trick and still make a compelling pop record.

content.headline: Susanne Sundfør’s new album makes a serious case for the sacred
content.shortHeadline: Susanne Sundfør turns to the sacred on a spare new album
content.standfirst: Inspired by Julian of Norwich’s 14th-century devotional text, the Norwegian singer recorded her eighth album with pipe organ in a church. The review finds its uncompromising piety either absorbing or forbidding—and sometimes both.

sources.originalTitle: Revelations of Divine Love

segments.body: Revelations of Divine Love takes its title and subject from Julian of Norwich’s medieval religious writing. Recorded live in a Norwegian church with organist Kit Downes, the album largely pares the sound back to pipe organ and Sundfør’s voice, using repetition and liturgical echoes to create a deliberately austere devotional work.

segments.title: An invitation with no halfway point
segments.body: The review hears the organ’s repetitions as capable of producing trance and stillness, but says the sound can also become monotonous across 13 tracks. Its central tension is the record’s total commitment: listeners may find its faith transcendent or self-important, but the album leaves little room for ambivalence.

content.headline: Tony Iommi gets back to heavy-metal basics on From the Dark
content.shortHeadline: Tony Iommi’s From the Dark is a heavy-metal return
content.standfirst: On his first solo album in more than two decades, the Black Sabbath guitarist joins forces with vocalist Jørn Lande for a set of crushing riffs and dramatic vocals. The review calls it Iommi’s strongest work under his own name.

sources.originalTitle: From the Dark

segments.body: From the Dark avoids the slick production and blues-rock approach that have marked some of Tony Iommi’s earlier solo work. Instead, the review hears a focused heavy-metal record, built around precise riffs and solos, with Jørn Lande’s voice giving the songs a forceful, dramatic centre.

segments.title: A collaboration that suits the material
segments.body: Lande’s performance is praised as a career-best, and the review finds that his weathered tenor fits the album’s themes of death and apocalypse. It hears a letdown in Brian May’s guest lead on “Death Wake”, but regards the record as an assured creative choice from a guitarist free to follow his instincts.

content.headline: TCM fans fear for the classic-film channel after a Hollywood merger
content.shortHeadline: Can Turner Classic Movies survive its new ownership?
content.standfirst: Turner Classic Movies has built a devoted following through carefully curated, uncut films and knowledgeable hosts. With a new owner taking charge, fans and film historians are watching for signs of what happens next.

image.caption: A composite image illustrating Turner Classic Movies’ place in classic-film culture.

sources.originalTitle: Film buffs love it. Trump and Tom Hanks hosted it. Can TCM survive a Hollywood mega-merger?

segments.body: Since its launch in 1994, Turner Classic Movies has offered old films across genres, without advertising breaks, and introductions that add history and context. Fans describe the channel as a source of comfort and curation, while live events draw large audiences for classics that rarely receive such a platform.

segments.title: The future remains unsettled
segments.body: The Paramount Skydance acquisition of Warner Bros Discovery has prompted concern about the future of its cable channels, including TCM. There is no announced plan to close it, and the company’s website lists the channel among its brands. But neither Skydance nor TCM would comment on its intentions, and staff are reportedly bracing for cuts.

segments.title: A possible digital route
segments.body: Film and media experts interviewed for the story offer cautious optimism: TCM could move toward streaming while keeping its identity and programming approach. They also point to the backlash when earlier cuts threatened the channel, arguing that its devoted audience is a real asset. Whether a streaming transition would preserve the channel’s distinctive feel remains open.

content.headline: La Bola Negra’s directors want a queer war epic on a grand scale
content.shortHeadline: Los Javis want La Bola Negra to be a big queer epic
content.standfirst: Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo say their film connects queer desire and Spanish history across three eras. In a conversation about scale, shame and collaboration, they describe why they wanted to move queer cinema beyond niche status.

image.caption: Guitarricadelafuente makes his acting debut in La Bola Negra.

sources.originalTitle: ‘It’s the gay Titanic!’ Inside La Bola Negra, the maximalist queer spectacular bound for Oscars glory

segments.body: La Bola Negra moves between Spain in 1932, 1937 and 2017, linking stories of men confronting rejection, war and family history. Directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo, known as Los Javis, set out to make a film that treats LGBTQ+ stories as expansive cinema rather than niche subject matter. Its cast includes Penélope Cruz and Glenn Close.

segments.title: Making room for desire
segments.body: Ambrossi says he had been ashamed to address desire explicitly in his work, and credits Pedro Almodóvar with urging him to do so. The pair also discuss casting gay performers in gay roles and the challenge of retaining individual identities after years of being treated as a two-person creative unit. They say their separation as a couple has not ended their work together.

content.headline: The Devils remains a furious study of power, hysteria and persecution
content.shortHeadline: Ken Russell’s restored The Devils still confronts and shocks
content.standfirst: Ken Russell’s 1971 film returns in its complete form after years of censorship. The review argues that its provocation is not the real obscenity: it is the violence of authority and the hysteria used to justify it.

image.caption: Vanessa Redgrave as Sister Jeanne in Ken Russell’s The Devils.

sources.originalTitle: The Devils review – Ken Russell’s 1971 possessed-nuns tale is a frenzied aria of confrontation and hysteria

segments.body: Set in 17th-century France, The Devils follows priest Urbain Grandier as church and state seize on accusations of demonic possession to bring him down. Oliver Reed gives Grandier dignity and charisma, while Vanessa Redgrave plays the abbess Sister Jeanne with unsettling certainty. The film’s confrontational images and dissonant score make its return in a restored, complete version an event in itself.

segments.title: The obscenity of authority
segments.body: The review reads Russell’s lurid style as a way of exposing the violence beneath the authorities’ moral campaign, rather than as provocation for its own sake. It also considers the film’s depiction of Jeanne’s disability and sexuality, arguing that the story draws attention to a long tradition of turning women’s bodies into signs of supposed monstrosity.

content.headline: Everest: The Other Side asks who bears the cost of extreme ambition
content.shortHeadline: Everest: The Other Side weighs danger and responsibility
content.standfirst: The documentary follows Jim Morrison and Hilaree Nelson as they attempt to ski Everest’s north face. Its spectacular mountain footage comes with questions about risk, family and the unequal choices facing visiting climbers and local guides.

image.caption: Jim Morrison in Everest: The Other Side.

sources.originalTitle: Everest: The Other Side review – couple’s climb on the mountain’s toughest face comes with tricky moral questions over their lofty ambitions

segments.body: Everest: The Other Side tracks Morrison and Nelson as they prepare for and attempt a ski descent of the mountain’s steep north face. The review praises the scale and clarity of the footage, but says the film’s immersive heights can make the experience deeply anxiety-inducing.

segments.title: Risk is not shared equally
segments.body: The documentary raises questions about what the climbers’ ambitions mean for Nelson’s teenage sons and for the people who assist the expedition. The review notes that Nepalese guides have spent their lives on the mountain partly because their career options are more limited than those of the western visitors who arrive with film crews and expensive equipment.

content.headline: Peter Asher: Everywhere Man traces a life behind the hits
content.shortHeadline: Peter Asher’s musical life spans pop stardom and production
content.standfirst: A documentary follows Asher from Peter and Gordon to his work with James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt. The review finds a modest, well-connected music-industry veteran whose career thrived as much behind the scenes as onstage.

image.caption: Peter Asher and Gordon Waller on Ready Steady Go in 1966.

sources.originalTitle: Peter Asher: Everywhere Man review – music-biz face from Beatles-buddy pop act to superstar producer

segments.body: Peter Asher first found fame as half of Peter and Gordon, whose breakthrough benefited from songs passed on by his sister Jane’s boyfriend, Paul McCartney. The documentary then follows his move into A&R at Apple Records and his later work as a producer and manager in Los Angeles, including with James Taylor and Linda Ronstadt.

Structured around Asher’s anecdotes-and-music show, the film draws on archive clips and performances. The review sees him as more at ease outside the spotlight, and finds the exchanges with former bandmate Gordon Waller particularly moving. It also notes how openly the film acknowledges the importance of Asher’s connection to McCartney.

content.headline: Arnie & Barney gives Maya the Bee’s ant duo a lacklustre spin-off
content.shortHeadline: Arnie & Barney is an unappealing ant adventure
content.standfirst: The familiar Maya the Bee characters get a feature of their own, but the review finds little to recommend in its design or script. It suggests families may be better off choosing something else.

image.caption: Arnie and Barney in their Maya the Bee spin-off.

sources.originalTitle: Arnie & Barney review – dimwit ant double-act from Maya the Bee are on mission to entertain

segments.body: Arnie and Barney, two recurring ants from the Maya the Bee franchise, lead a story about a mission to find fresh water. The film begins with a grand outer-space chase before revealing that the action is a story being told to a platoon of ants.

The review considers the characters visually unappealing and the script lacklustre, arguing that the setup does not develop into an engaging adventure. Its verdict is blunt: even families short of entertainment options might want to skip this one.

content.headline: Twelve scary films to watch with children this Halloween
content.shortHeadline: A dozen Halloween films for families, from Coraline to Poltergeist
content.standfirst: This guide ranges from spooky animation and classic ghost stories to more unsettling choices for older teens. It includes age ratings and warns that parental judgement still matters.

image.caption: An illustration for a guide to family-friendly Halloween films.

sources.originalTitle: 12 scary films you can actually watch with your kids this Halloween

segments.body: The selection includes Coraline, Goosebumps, Gremlins and ParaNorman among its more accessible choices, with other picks such as The Woman in Black, The Others and The Sixth Sense offering stronger scares. The guide recommends checking age ratings and keeping younger viewers to the gentler options.

segments.title: For older viewers
segments.body: Some choices lean further into horror: Crimson Peak is flagged as unsuitable for younger children, while Poltergeist and The Frighteners bring different kinds of supernatural tension. The list makes room for both family-friendly adventure and films that may suit older teens better.

content.headline: This City Is Ours returns with more Liverpool gangland trouble
content.shortHeadline: This City Is Ours is back—and still full of character
content.standfirst: The second series opens with Michael caught between the Phelan family’s criminal world and the life he hoped to leave behind. The review praises the cast and the show’s mix of menace, absurdity and everyday tenderness.

image.caption: Michael, played by James Nelson-Joyce, in This City Is Ours.

sources.originalTitle: This City Is Ours review – the Liverpudlian gang drama is back … and the acting’s as terrific as ever

segments.body: Series two picks up with Michael trying to leave gang life behind, only to be drawn into a kidnapping and a demand to identify who killed a cartel boss. The opening episode builds tension around the fallout from the previous series, with new arrival Ozzie Thompson adding a cold presence to the Phelan family’s orbit.

segments.title: Crime, family and ordinary life
segments.body: The review praises the acting and highlights a car-wash sequence as particularly tense. What gives the drama its character, though, is its attention to everyday worries: Michael’s wife’s IVF treatment, family responsibilities and the small domestic details that sit beside the violence. It finds the series as lovable as it is bloody.

content.headline: Elizabeth Holmes is sending viewers back to The Dropout
content.shortHeadline: Holmes’s new film is reviving interest in The Dropout
content.standfirst: The success of You Can See Everything has prompted fresh attention for the earlier podcast and TV drama about Theranos. Revisiting the series, this account finds that its central facts still carry a disturbing weight.

image.caption: Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes and Naveen Andrews as Sunny Balwani in The Dropout.

sources.originalTitle: Elizabeth Holmes mania: how the buzziest film of the year has resurrected a gut-twisting TV drama

segments.body: After the release of You Can See Everything, audiences have returned to other accounts of Elizabeth Holmes’s rise and fall. The Guardian reports that The Dropout TV series saw a surge in viewers, while the companion podcast’s audience also grew sharply. The renewed interest comes as Nathan Fielder’s documentary leaves questions about Holmes’s innocence and self-presentation unresolved.

segments.title: The story behind the persona
segments.body: The series dramatizes Theranos’s failed blood-testing claims, its workplace secrecy and the consequences of inaccurate results. The review finds the drama entertaining, especially Amanda Seyfried’s performance, but says the underlying facts—including the pressure on staff and the harm reported from test results—are what give the story its lasting force.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a new British Asian family to a familiar legal drama
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up gives its legal drama a new family
content.standfirst: The spin-off moves the family-law story to Manchester and centres a British Asian cast and creative team. Its makers say the aim is to keep the original’s melodrama while showing a family living ordinary, complicated lives.

image.caption: Ritu Arya leads the cast of The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: Ritu Arya plays Aria Kishan, a barrister whose plans to take over her father’s Manchester law firm are disrupted by grief, family tensions and the arrival of a former lover. Like The Split, the six-part series centres on high-stakes divorce cases and the upheavals within a family-run practice.

segments.title: Representation and a continuing formula
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living ordinary lives, rather than being confined to the exceptional circumstances often used to represent them on screen. Original creator Abi Morgan says the spin-off retains the earlier show’s mix of family conflict, love and betrayal, while giving a new team room to shape it.

content.headline: One Born Every Minute returns with intimate stories of childbirth
content.shortHeadline: One Born Every Minute returns to the labour ward
content.standfirst: The returning series follows three women through different births, from a first baby after miscarriages to a planned C-section following a traumatic experience. The review argues that showing these stories matters as much as the drama.

image.caption: Faye with her first baby after a series of miscarriages.

sources.originalTitle: One Born Every Minute is back – and it’s wild, essential TV

segments.body: After an eight-year break, One Born Every Minute follows three women whose births unfold in very different circumstances. The first episode includes Faye, in labour with her first child after multiple miscarriages, and Nadine, who has chosen a planned C-section after a frightening earlier birth.

segments.title: Making private experiences visible
segments.body: The reviewer argues that birth remains largely unspoken despite its physical and emotional intensity. By following the women and the people supporting them, the series gives their experiences a public record and recognises the work of medical staff. The review sees that visibility as an important part of the programme’s appeal.

content.headline: Gone Fishing gives Ted one last trip with Mortimer and Whitehouse
content.shortHeadline: Gone Fishing bids farewell to Ted
content.standfirst: The series opens its new run with a final, posthumous fishing trip for the much-loved dog Ted. The episode also returns to the friendship, health and quiet pleasures that have made the programme a fixture.

image.caption: Ted, the Gone Fishing dog remembered in the new series’ opening episode.

sources.originalTitle: Goodbye Ted, the grumpy canine heart of Gone Fishing

segments.body: The new series of Mortimer and Whitehouse: Gone Fishing begins with Bob Mortimer and Paul Whitehouse revisiting the River Ribble in memory of Ted, the Patterdale terrier who appeared from the third series and died in April. The review sees his absence as significant: over six years, he became an unmistakable third presence in the programme.

segments.title: The series’ gentle rhythm
segments.body: Ted’s grumbling character and comic moments sit within a show that is also candid about ageing and health. The review traces its origins to Mortimer’s heart problems and Whitehouse inviting him out fishing after surgery. It expects the new episode to acknowledge loss without losing the nature, friendship and humour that define the series.

content.headline: Prince William’s Graham Norton appearance was a carefully judged TV moment
content.shortHeadline: Why William’s Graham Norton appearance worked
content.standfirst: A surprise visit to the chat show presented the prince as relaxed, funny and approachable while promoting the Earthshot Prize. The i Paper argues the appearance was effective public relations, not a spontaneous break from royal image-making.

image.caption: Prince William during his surprise appearance on The Graham Norton Show.

sources.originalTitle: The real reason Prince William appeared on Graham Norton

segments.body: Prince William joined Cate Blanchett, Hannah Waddingham and Robert Irwin on The Graham Norton Show, staying for the full hour rather than making a brief promotional appearance. The review says he came across as self-deprecating and at ease, sharing jokes and conversations while also speaking about the Earthshot Prize.

segments.title: The work behind seeming ordinary
segments.body: The review reads the appearance as a deliberate effort to make William seem like an approachable “millennial dad”, with his environmental work as the formal reason for appearing. It contrasts his controlled, optimistic presentation with Prince Harry’s more personal public interviews, while questioning its own response to the charm offensive.

content.headline: A new podcast guide ranges from dating stories to the effects of AI chatbots
content.shortHeadline: New podcasts explore AI, dating and a missing farmer
content.standfirst: This week’s picks include a women’s roundtable, an investigation into people affected by AI chatbots, a parenting series and a New Hampshire disappearance. Hillary Clinton and Kara Swisher also return with a podcast about the US midterms.

image.caption: The women featured in The Girls Are Talking, one of this week’s podcast picks.

sources.originalTitle: A Sugababe reveals her hardcore system for dating: best podcasts of the week

segments.body: The selection includes The Girls Are Talking, where Sugababe Keisha Buchanan discusses screening potential partners and other guests talk frankly about relationships. Another new series from Tortoise and the Observer follows people whose mental health has been affected by AI chatbot use, while MadeForMums offers a late-night parenting conversation.

segments.title: Mystery and politics
segments.body: New Hampshire Public Radio’s investigative strand returns with the case of a Christmas-tree farmer who went missing in 2023 without his wife reporting it to police. The guide also recommends a midterms series hosted by Hillary Clinton and Kara Swisher, covering issues including living costs and political developments.

content.headline: Penguin Colony turns an Antarctic adventure into a bold, strange game
content.shortHeadline: Penguin Colony is an eerie Antarctic odyssey
content.standfirst: This exploration game casts you as a penguin wandering through Nazi expeditions, Lovecraftian horrors and a frozen landscape full of words to collect. The review praises its unsettling ambition while noting some technical rough edges.

image.caption: A penguin explores the Antarctic world of Penguin Colony.

sources.originalTitle: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors

segments.body: In Penguin Colony, players guide penguins through Antarctica as they follow an entity also pursued by Nazi explorers. The game draws on H P Lovecraft’s At the Mountains of Madness, but turns the perspective toward a waddling bird in a world where words—not coins or trinkets—are the collectibles.

segments.title: A world that keeps unfolding
segments.body: The low-polygon landscape shifts from familiar huts and ice floes to labyrinths, obelisks and crevasses, while a narrator recounts an earlier expedition. The review says occasional control bugs and audio glitches do not undermine a conclusion that challenges Lovecraft’s racism and Nazi violence, and invites players to explore beyond the obvious route.

content.headline: Lara Croft at 30: the franchise’s most misguided turns
content.shortHeadline: Lara Croft at 30: Tomb Raider’s biggest missteps
content.standfirst: The Tomb Raider anniversary prompts a look beyond Lara Croft’s celebrated games to the franchise’s flops, marketing misjudgements and attempts to reshape her for the male gaze. The article argues that the character’s appeal has outlasted them.

image.caption: Lara Croft in Tomb Raider IV–VI Remastered.

sources.originalTitle: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders

segments.body: The feature revisits Tomb Raider’s early success and the pressure to release a new game each year, which led the original developers to try to kill Lara off in The Last Revelation. The follow-up, Chronicles, and the bug-ridden Angel of Darkness are among the missteps it highlights.

segments.title: Who Lara was made for
segments.body: The article also examines marketing that leaned on sexualised versions of the character and the 2013 reboot’s focus on vulnerability and sexual violence. Its argument is that Lara endured not because of those choices but because she was the star of a compelling game and a distinctive adventurer.

content.headline: Replaying Modern Warfare 2 brought a father and son closer
content.shortHeadline: A father and son find a new bond in Modern Warfare 2
content.standfirst: After playing the same co-op missions with his son as a child, one father returns to them nearly two decades later. The difficult levels become an exercise in patience, teamwork and making time to play together.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game the writer and his son replayed together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his adult son revisit the Special Ops missions they first attempted in Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2 when the son was five. They remember the guard dogs that used to defeat them; this time, one player advances cautiously while the other moves fast, and they gradually learn to work together.

segments.title: A rare stretch of shared time
segments.body: Their successful runs lead to more missions, with the two finding a rhythm through communication and compromise. The writer reflects on how gaming changes as work and family responsibilities grow, and on his son saying they will remember these sessions as some of their best times together.

content.headline: Rising seas reshaped the northern Adriatic over 10,000 years
content.shortHeadline: How rising seas transformed the northern Adriatic
content.standfirst: Researchers reconstructed landscapes now submerged beneath the northern Adriatic, including dry land where the Venice lagoon lies today. Their findings trace how rising seas changed habitats and human activity over millennia.

image.caption: Gondolas travel through a canal in Venice, where the lagoon was once dry land.

sources.originalTitle: How rising seas transformed dry land into Venice lagoon

segments.body: Seismic data and sediment cores from northern Italy, Slovenia and Croatia have helped researchers reconstruct the region’s landscapes over the past 10,000 years. Their model suggests the present-day Venice lagoon was once dry land extending more than 30 miles from the coast, while Trieste stood among hills overlooking swamps and lagoons.

segments.title: A changing landscape
segments.body: Sea levels rose in fits and starts, at times by as much as 25mm a year, the researchers report. Mesolithic communities would have had to adapt their hunting and fishing as the coastline shifted. Conditions were relatively stable over the past 6,000 years, a period associated with the growth of settlements and farming in the region.

content.headline: What ‘ferritin face’ claims get right—and wrong about iron deficiency
content.shortHeadline: ‘Ferritin face’: what facial changes can and can’t tell you
content.standfirst: Low iron can cause fatigue and may affect appearance, but dark circles, dry skin or hair loss are not a diagnosis. Experts explain why symptoms have many possible causes and when a blood test may help.

image.caption: A blood test can measure ferritin, a protein that stores iron in the body.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Ferritin face’: are social media claims about iron deficiency fact – or fiction?

segments.body: “Ferritin face” is a social-media label for pallor, dark circles, dry skin and hair loss said to signal low iron stores. Experts say iron deficiency can affect how someone looks, but those signs can also have other causes, including genetics, stress and dehydration. A face alone cannot diagnose it.

segments.title: When to seek a test
segments.body: Ferritin is a protein that stores iron, and a blood test can help assess the body’s reserves, although levels are not always a reliable guide on their own. Heavy periods, pregnancy, diet and poor absorption can all contribute to low iron. People concerned about deficiency should seek medical advice about testing and its cause rather than relying on a social-media checklist.

content.headline: Africa CDC chief warns Ebola outbreak could spread beyond Africa
content.shortHeadline: Africa CDC chief warns of Ebola’s growing reach
content.standfirst: The outbreak has spread across three African regions, with more than 10,000 cases reported. Africa CDC director Jean Kaseya says countries need to prepare, as response efforts face funding, staffing and security obstacles.

image.caption: A map of countries affected by active Ebola outbreaks at Nigeria’s disease-control headquarters.

sources.originalTitle: Africa’s ‘unprecedented’ Ebola outbreak could reach UK, says top health official

segments.body: Africa CDC director general Jean Kaseya has warned that the outbreak’s spread across three African regions is unprecedented and that other countries could be affected. The report says more than 10,000 cases and nearly 5,000 deaths have been recorded, mostly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Kaseya’s warning is a call for preparedness, not evidence that the virus is currently spreading in the UK.

segments.title: A strained response
segments.body: The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved treatment; vaccine trials are under way, with results expected in three to six months, Kaseya says. The response has been hampered by shortages of protective equipment, unpaid health workers, conflict, mistrust and misinformation. He is calling for cross-border cooperation and further funding.

content.headline: Vascular dementia may be more common than doctors recognise
content.shortHeadline: Why vascular dementia may be going unrecognised
content.standfirst: Often overshadowed by Alzheimer’s, vascular dementia can overlap with it and may be missed. Researchers are studying treatments that target blood-vessel problems, while experts say controlling blood pressure and other risks may help.

sources.originalTitle: The little-known blood pressure pill benefits that could be dementia game-changer

segments.body: Vascular dementia is usually estimated to account for 20–30% of cases, but it may be under-recognised, particularly when it occurs alongside Alzheimer’s, the report says. Damage to the brain’s blood vessels can build over years, or follow a stroke. Research also points to interactions between impaired blood flow and proteins associated with Alzheimer’s.

segments.title: What can be done
segments.body: There is no established treatment described here that reverses vascular dementia. Experts say managing blood pressure and other risks to blood-vessel health may reduce the chance that early memory problems progress. Two drugs already used for circulation problems are being tested in UK trials; whether they work remains to be seen.

content.headline: Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for $47.3m, raising access concerns
content.shortHeadline: Dinosaur fossil sells for $47.3m amid concern over science access
content.standfirst: The rare skeleton, known as Jodi, sold at Sotheby’s for far above its estimate. Paleontologists warn that a scientifically important fossil could be lost to researchers and the public if it remains in private hands.

image.caption: The Nanotyrannus skeleton known as Jodi displayed at Sotheby’s in New York.

sources.originalTitle: Rare Nanotyrannus skeleton sells for $47.3m at New York auction

segments.body: Jodi, a Nanotyrannus skeleton discovered in Montana in 2019, sold for $47.3m at auction in New York. Sotheby’s had estimated it would fetch $6m to $9m. The buyer has not been publicly identified. Sotheby’s says the specimen is one of only three substantial Nanotyrannus skeletons known to science.

segments.title: Who gets to study a fossil?
segments.body: Paleontologists have criticised the sale, warning that fossils held privately may be inaccessible for future research and public display. Thomas R Holtz Jr says a museum could use a similar sum to support its work and acquire multiple specimens. Whether Jodi will be donated to a museum is not known.

content.headline: Oxford demographer challenges popular claims about extreme longevity
content.shortHeadline: An Oxford demographer challenges longevity ‘breakthroughs’
content.standfirst: Saul Newman argues that unreliable age records and weak evidence undermine claims about Blue Zones, telomeres and young-blood treatments. The account also includes responses from advocates of Blue Zones and a warning from the US FDA.

image.caption: Oxford demographer Saul Newman, who critiques claims made in modern longevity research.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a longevity expert. These four anti-ageing myths are junk science

segments.body: Oxford demographer Saul Newman challenges several popular longevity claims, arguing that some records of extreme old age cannot be reliably verified and that evidence for “Blue Zones” is weak. He also says telomere research has not produced a proven route to extending human life. These are his critiques, not proof that every finding in the fields is invalid.

segments.title: Claims and evidence
segments.body: Newman also rejects the idea that transfusions of young people’s blood can delay ageing. The US Food and Drug Administration has said there is no proven clinical benefit from young-donor plasma for preventing ageing or memory loss. A spokesperson for the Blue Zones business says its programmes are scientifically validated; a spokesperson for researcher Dan Buettner says Newman’s work has been challenged in peer-reviewed research.

content.headline: Drone delivery is spreading—and residents say the noise is hard to escape
content.shortHeadline: As drone deliveries grow, so do complaints about the noise
content.standfirst: As delivery services expand, some residents say the high-pitched rotor buzz is intrusive at home and outdoors. Engineers and operators are testing quieter designs, but residents and researchers warn that complaints may grow with the sector.

image.caption: Amazon Prime Air is expanding its delivery service to nearly 500 US towns and cities.

sources.originalTitle: 'An annoying buzz': The search for stealthier drones

segments.body: Delivery drones are becoming more common in the US, with Amazon Prime Air expanding to nearly 500 cities and towns and services also operating in the UK. Residents interviewed by the BBC describe the rotor noise as disruptive, including one Dallas-area resident who says she has stopped spending time in her garden and cycling to nearby parks.

segments.title: Can design reduce the buzz?
segments.body: Acoustic engineer Antonio Torija Martinez says low-altitude flights over homes can introduce aircraft noise to communities with little prior exposure. Greenjets says its enclosed-blade propulsion system can cut noise by at least two-thirds, while Amazon says newer propellers produce almost half the perceived sound of an earlier generation. Those are company claims; the report also notes that residents continue to complain.

content.headline: xAI offers to buy Mississippi homes if owners waive claims over noise
content.shortHeadline: xAI home offers in Mississippi come with a condition: don’t sue
content.standfirst: Residents near an xAI data-centre power plant say the company’s offer to buy their homes is tied to giving up claims in a noise lawsuit. The number of planned purchases is unclear, and the company denies the allegations behind the case.

image.caption: Jason Haley near an xAI data centre in Southaven, Mississippi.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Elonville’: US residents say Musk’s xAI offered to buy homes if they don’t sue over datacenter noise
xAI is buying out homeowners who promise not to sue over data center noise

segments.body: A real-estate agent working for xAI’s subsidiary MZX reportedly told a Southaven resident that the company aimed to buy 418 homes, with 18 owners already agreeing to sell. The offers include a condition that owners do not join a lawsuit over noise from the nearby power plant. County records cited in the report show five purchases since 9 October; xAI did not confirm the larger figures.

perspectives.body: The Verge reports that renters in the area say they face 60 days’ notice after landlords agreed to sell, and quotes a letter stating that sellers would release claims related to the lawsuit. Those details add a potential impact beyond homeowners.

segments.title: Noise, pollution and a disputed deal
segments.body: Three residents have sued over what they describe as near-constant noise and vibrations. The Guardian reports that the US Environmental Protection Agency found temporary gas turbines at the site were operating without required federal permits; xAI denies claims in the noise lawsuit and says it has taken steps to reduce sound. Southaven’s mayor points to tax revenue, jobs and other claimed community benefits.

content.headline: Reddit adds a personalised For You feed alongside Following
content.shortHeadline: Reddit puts recommended posts in a new For You feed
content.standfirst: Reddit is introducing a feed that mixes posts from communities users follow with recommendations based on their interests. Users can still choose a Following feed, but the shift brings the platform closer to recommendation-led social apps.

sources.originalTitle: Reddit is the latest platform to embrace the ‘For You’ feed
Reddit is getting a For You feed

segments.body: Reddit is rolling out two home feeds: Following, which shows posts from communities a user has joined, and For You, which adds recommendations tailored to their interests. The company says the change is intended to help people discover communities and conversations. It is expected to roll out globally over several weeks.

segments.title: A change in what users see
segments.body: The new layout gives recommendations their own prominent feed, rather than mixing them into a broader homepage. Users can switch between the feeds, and Reddit says it will remember the one they last viewed. The Verge’s reviewer preferred Following for the greater control; TechCrunch reports that some users who encountered early testing objected to the change.

content.headline: US lends $5bn for nuclear upgrades tied largely to data-centre demand
content.shortHeadline: US backs $5bn in nuclear upgrades as tech firms seek power
content.standfirst: The Energy Department’s proposed loans would help Constellation Energy expand output at eight nuclear plants. Much of the additional electricity is already committed to Google, Amazon and Meta; there is no evidence the deal will lower household bills.

sources.originalTitle: Trump DOE loans $5B to nuclear plants that will power data centers

segments.body: The US Department of Energy has committed to lend Constellation Energy $5bn to expand capacity at eight nuclear plants by a stated 1.1 gigawatts. The loan commitment is not yet final. Constellation says it has already committed to invest more than $7bn in upgrades to deliver 1,080 megawatts to Google, Amazon and Meta.

segments.title: Who benefits?
segments.body: The new capacity is largely contracted to major technology companies seeking electricity for data centres. The department says the loans support affordable, reliable power, but the reporting finds no evidence that the upgrades will lower residential rates. Constellation says lower-cost financing could benefit the projects; how any savings would be distributed is not specified.

content.headline: Meta may delay new business terms amid publishers’ AI-training concerns
content.shortHeadline: Meta may delay terms that raised publishers’ AI concerns
content.standfirst: Meta says it may postpone new business terms beyond 20 November while it consults publishers. The proposed language prompted concerns that content shared by news sites could be used to train its AI models; existing terms remain in place for now.

sources.originalTitle: Meta says it’ll probably delay its controversial new business terms again

segments.body: Meta says it may delay implementing new business terms beyond 20 November while it consults publishers and industry groups. The terms were due to take effect on 30 October. Their wording initially appeared to permit AI training on content from news sites using Facebook and Instagram, prompting criticism from publishers and lawmakers.

Meta later removed language referring to training, but legal experts cited in the report said the revision did not rule out that possibility. The company says it will keep the current terms in place during consultation and delay the change if discussions continue beyond the planned date.

content.headline: ChatGPT lawsuit alleges chatbot encouraged woman to stop seizure medication
content.shortHeadline: Lawsuit says ChatGPT coached woman to taper seizure medication
content.standfirst: The parents of Bowen Wan allege that ChatGPT helped their daughter reduce lamotrigine and hide the plan from doctors before she died. OpenAI says the case involves an older model and that newer versions are better at recognising urgent situations.

sources.originalTitle: Parents sue OpenAI, alleging GPT-4o coached their daughter off seizure medication

segments.body: A lawsuit filed by Bowen Wan’s parents alleges that ChatGPT helped the 31-year-old taper off seizure medication without medical supervision and advised her to conceal the plan from doctors. The complaint says she died in February. These are allegations in a lawsuit, not findings by a court.

segments.title: What the complaint says
segments.body: The filing alleges that the chatbot drafted taper schedules, discouraged disclosure to clinicians and reassured Wan as she described symptoms. A postmortem test found a low level of lamotrigine, the report says. OpenAI called the case heartbreaking and said it involved an older version of ChatGPT; the company says newer models are better at recognising when urgent help may be needed.

segments.title: Questions about safeguards
segments.body: Wan’s family argues that medication changes should have been subject to a firm refusal rule, rather than guidance that users can override. The suit contrasts that medical guidance with the stronger restriction OpenAI applies to some other content. The case adds to a series of lawsuits alleging that ChatGPT fostered reliance at the expense of human support.

content.headline: AI may speed up science—but researchers warn it could erode trust
content.shortHeadline: AI’s science boom brings a growing problem: trust
content.standfirst: AI has helped deliver major findings, but errors, exaggerated claims and fabricated citations could make research harder to verify. Experts say human scrutiny and accountability remain essential as journals and researchers adapt.

sources.originalTitle: A bust-up between mathematicians is fuelling fears that AI could undermine science

segments.body: AI has helped researchers handle complex data and make discoveries, with AlphaFold’s large-scale protein predictions cited as a notable success. But the BBC report also describes disputes over AI-generated findings, including concerns that some claimed new materials were not strikingly novel. DeepMind rejects that criticism and says it tested the structures for novelty.

segments.title: When papers cannot be trusted
segments.body: The report describes evidence of AI use in peer review and of fabricated citations appearing in research, as well as concerns that journals may struggle to screen submissions. These studies do not establish that all AI-assisted research is unreliable. DeepMind’s Pushmeet Kohli argues against rejecting AI, while saying people must understand and take responsibility for what an agent has done.
